captions.instagram:
How does a thermos work?

A steel flask keeps chai hot from breakfast to teatime with nothing at all: a gap emptied of air, two mirror-bright walls and a good stopper. Block heat's three escape routes in 3D, run twelve hours in twenty seconds, and find out why a fizzy drink should never go in one.

→ A vacuum flask is a bottle inside a bottle, with the air pumped out of the gap between them.
→ Fill the gap with air and 90 °C chai loses 12 watts by conduction. Pump it out and that falls to a few hundredths.
→ A vacuum can't stop the infrared glow. Shiny walls can: dull ones would leak 15 watts.
→ Twelve hours in twenty seconds: boiling water in a jug is cold by lunch. In the flask it is still about 60 °C.
→ Half-full, the flask leaks almost as much heat but stores half as much, so it cools twice as fast.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/thermosclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a thermos work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A steel flask keeps chai hot from breakfast to teatime with nothing at all: a gap emptied of air, two mirror-bright walls and a good stopper. Block heat's three escape routes in 3D, run twelve hours in twenty seconds, and find out why a fizzy drink should never go in one.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/thermosclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/thermosclear

In this video:
• A bottle inside a bottle. A vacuum flask is two bottles, one inside the other, joined only in a thin ring at the neck.
• Three escapes, three blocks. Heat leaves by conduction, convection and radiation.
• The real leaks: neck and stopper. Where the vacuum can't reach, heat still gets out: along the neck, where the walls are joined, and through the stopper.
• Slow cooling, not no cooling. A flask cools along the same curve as any hot drink, about twenty times more slowly than a jug with a lid.
• Making and losing the vacuum. Removing half the air does nothing: conduction only falls once the gas is so thin that molecules cross the gap without meeting, below about 1 pascal.
• Use it safely. Hot drinks in a flask stay hot enough to scald for hours.
